title: Discrete Random Variables and Expectation
summary: Outcomes of experiments are often not numbers (a card, a sequence of tosses), but we usually care about a numerical summary: the number of heads, the sum of two dice, the waiting time for the first success. A random variable is the bridge between outcomes…

intro.x: Outcomes of experiments are often not numbers (a card, a sequence of tosses), but we usually care about a numerical summary: the number of heads, the sum of two dice, the waiting time for the first success. A random variable is the bridge between outcomes and numbers. This chapter defines random variables on discrete sample spaces, introduces the probability mass function and the cumulative distribution function, and develops the central quantity of probability: the expectation.

blocks.x: Let $(\Omega,\F,\Prob)$ be a probability space. A random variable is a function $X:\Omega\to\R$ such that for every real $x$, the set $\{\omega:X(\omega)\le x\}$ is an event (that is, belongs to $\F$).

A random variable is neither random nor a variable: it is a function on the sample space, and the randomness comes from the outcome $\omega$ being random. The condition that $\{X\le x\}$ is an event guarantees that questions such as “what is the probability that $X\le x$?” make sense. When $\Omega$ is finite or countable and $\F=2^\Omega$, every function $X:\Omega\to\R$ satisfies this condition automatically, so for now we can ignore it. Chapter 15 revisits the condition.

A random variable $X$ is discrete if it takes values in a finite or countable set $\{x_1,x_2,\dots\}$. The smallest such set (the set of values with positive probability, together with possible limit points we shall not need) is called the support of $X$.
We use the shorthand $\{X=x\}$ for the event $\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)=x\}$ and write $\Prob(X=x)$, $\Prob(X\in A)$, $\Prob(X\le x)$ accordingly.
Roll two fair dice, $\Omega=\{1,\dots,6\}^2$. Let $S(i,j)=i+j$ and $M(i,j)=\max(i,j)$. Both are random variables. The event $\{S=4\}$ is $\{(1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\}$, with probability $3/36=1/12$.
For an event $A$, the indicator of $A$ is the random variable $\indic_A(\omega)=1$ if $\omega\in A$ and $0$ otherwise.

Indicators translate events into numbers. They satisfy $\indic_{A\cap B}=\indic_A\indic_B$, $\indic_{A^c}=1-\indic_A$, and $\indic_{A\cup B}=\indic_A+\indic_B-\indic_A\indic_B$. We will see that expressing a count as a sum of indicators is one of the most powerful techniques in the subject.

sections.title: Distribution: the mass function and the CDF

blocks.x: The probability mass function (PMF) of a discrete random variable $X$ is $p_X(x)=\Prob(X=x)$, for $x\in\R$.
The PMF satisfies $p_X(x)\ge0$, $p_X(x)>0$ for at most countably many $x$, and $\sum_xp_X(x)=1$. Moreover, for any $A\subseteq\R$, $\Prob(X\in A)=\sum_{x\in A}p_X(x)$.

The events $\{X=x\}$, $x$ in the countable value set, form a partition of $\Omega$. Apply countable additivity, first to the whole partition (giving the sum $1$) and then to the sub-collection with $x\in A$.
The PMF is the complete description of how $X$ is distributed; everything we need about $X$ alone can be computed from it. Two different random variables can have the same PMF.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: same distribution does not mean same random variable

blocks.x: Toss a fair coin. Let $X=1$ if heads, $0$ if tails, and $Y=1-X$. Then $X$ and $Y$ each have PMF $p(0)=p(1)=1/2$, so they have the same distribution, but $X(\omega)\ne Y(\omega)$ for every outcome $\omega$. We write $X\overset{d}{=}Y$ for “equal in distribution”. Equality in distribution says nothing about how two random variables are related on the same sample space; that information lives in the joint distribution (Chapter 6).
The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a random variable $X$ is $F_X(x)=\Prob(X\le x)$, for $x\in\R$.
The CDF is defined for every random variable, discrete or not, which is why it is the universal tool.
Let $F=F_X$. Then
$F$ is non-decreasing;
$\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}F(x)=1$;
$F$ is right-continuous: $\lim_{h\downarrow0}F(x+h)=F(x)$;
$\Prob(a<X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)$ for $a<b$;
$\Prob(X=x)=F(x)-F(x^-)$, where $F(x^-)=\lim_{h\downarrow0}F(x-h)$ is the left limit; hence $F$ jumps at $x$ by exactly $p_X(x)$.
(i) If $x\le y$ then $\{X\le x\}\subseteq\{X\le y\}$; apply monotonicity.

(ii) Let $x_n\to-\infty$ be any decreasing sequence. The events $\{X\le x_n\}$ decrease to $\bigcap_n\{X\le x_n\}=\emptyset$, since no real number $X(\omega)$ is below every $x_n$. By continuity of probability (Theorem 2.10), $F(x_n)\to\Prob(\emptyset)=0$. Because $F$ is monotone, the limit along any sequence equals the limit along all of $\R$. For $+\infty$, the events $\{X\le x_n\}$ with $x_n\uparrow\infty$ increase to $\Omega$, giving limit $1$.
(iii) Take $h_n\downarrow0$. The events $\{X\le x+h_n\}$ decrease to $\{X\le x\}$ (since $X(\omega)\le x+h_n$ for all $n$ if and only if $X(\omega)\le x$). Continuity from above gives the limit.
(iv) $\{X\le b\}$ is the disjoint union of $\{X\le a\}$ and $\{a<X\le b\}$.
(v) The events $\{X\le x-h_n\}$ increase to $\{X<x\}$. By continuity from below, $F(x^-)=\Prob(X<x)$, and $\Prob(X=x)=\Prob(X\le x)-\Prob(X<x)$.

The CDF uses “$\le$”, which makes it right-continuous; a CDF built with “$<$” would be left-continuous. When you evaluate a CDF at a jump, the value is the upper value of the jump. This is why $\Prob(a

Let $M=\max(i,j)$ for two fair dice. Then $\{M\le m\}$ is the event that both rolls are at most $m$, with probability $m^2/36$. So $F_M(m)=m^2/36$ for $m=1,\dots,6$, and by Theorem 4.8(v) the PMF is $p_M(m)=(m^2-(m-1)^2)/36=(2m-1)/36$.
Functions of a random variable

If $X$ is a random variable and $g:\R\to\R$ a function, then $Y=g(X)$ is a random variable (for discrete $X$ always; the general condition is in Chapter 15). Its PMF is obtained by adding up the masses of all $x$ that map to each $y$:
p_Y(y)=\Prob(g(X)=y)=\sum_{x:\,g(x)=y}p_X(x).
Let $X$ be uniform on $\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$ and $Y=X^2$. Then $Y\in\{0,1,4\}$ with $p_Y(0)=1/5$, $p_Y(1)=2/5$, $p_Y(4)=2/5$. Note that $g$ is not injective, so the masses of $x=\pm1$ merge.
The expectation is the probability-weighted average of the values of $X$.
Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with PMF $p_X$. If $\sum_x\abs{x}\,p_X(x)<\infty$, the expectation (or mean) of $X$ is
\Exp[X]=\sum_xx\,p_X(x).
We then say $X$ is integrable, written $\Exp\abs X<\infty$. If the condition fails, the expectation is not defined (with one exception: if $X\ge0$, we may write $\Exp[X]=+\infty$).

Why insist on $\sum\abs x p(x)<\infty$ rather than just convergence of $\sum xp(x)$? A conditionally convergent series can be rearranged to converge to any number (Riemann’s rearrangement theorem). The mean must not depend on the order in which we list the values of $X$, and absolute convergence is exactly what guarantees this. Concretely, take $\Prob(X=(-1)^{k}k)=c/k^2$ for $k=1,2,\dots$ with $c=6/\pi^2$; then $\sum xp(x)=c\sum(-1)^k/k$ converges, but $\sum\abs xp(x)=c\sum1/k=\infty$, and we declare $\Exp[X]$ undefined.
Toss a fair coin until the first head, at toss $K$, and receive $2^K$ rupees. Then $\Prob(K=k)=2^{-k}$ and the payoff $X=2^K$ is non-negative with
\Exp[X]=\sum_{k=1}^\infty2^k\cdot2^{-k}=\sum_{k=1}^\infty1=+\infty.

The game has infinite expected payoff, yet nobody would pay a large sum to play. Resolutions include limited bankroll or diminishing marginal utility (Bernoulli’s suggestion to use $\Exp[\log X]$). Note also that $X<\infty$ with probability $1$: infinite expectation does not mean the payoff itself is infinite.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Law of the unconscious statistician, LOTUS

blocks.x: Let $X$ be discrete and $g:\R\to\R$. If $\sum_x\abs{g(x)}p_X(x)<\infty$, then
\Exp[g(X)]=\sum_xg(x)\,p_X(x).
Let $Y=g(X)$. Group the values $x$ according to $y=g(x)$:

\sum_xg(x)p_X(x)=\sum_y\sum_{x:\,g(x)=y}y\,p_X(x)=\sum_yy\sum_{x:\,g(x)=y}p_X(x)
=\sum_yy\,p_Y(y)=\Exp[Y].
Regrouping is legitimate because the series converges absolutely.
LOTUS says we can compute $\Exp[g(X)]$ from the distribution of $X$ without first finding the distribution of $g(X)$.
If $\Omega$ is countable with $p(\omega)=\Prob(\{\omega\})$, then $\Exp[X]=\sum_{\omega}X(\omega)p(\omega)$, whenever $\sum_\omega\abs{X(\omega)}p(\omega)<\infty$.
Group the outcomes by the value of $X$: $\sum_\omega X(\omega)p(\omega)= \sum_xx\sum_{\omega:X(\omega)=x}p(\omega)=\sum_xx\,p_X(x)$.
Let $X,Y$ be integrable random variables on a countable sample space and $a,b\in\R$. Then $aX+bY$ is integrable and
\Exp[aX+bY]=a\Exp[X]+b\Exp[Y].
No assumption about the relationship between $X$ and $Y$ (in particular, no independence) is needed.
By Proposition 4.14,

\Exp[aX+bY]=\sum_\omega(aX(\omega)+bY(\omega))p(\omega)
=a\sum_\omega X(\omega)p(\omega)+b\sum_\omega Y(\omega)p(\omega),
where splitting the series is valid because both converge absolutely. Absolute convergence of the left side follows from $\abs{aX+bY}\le\abs a\abs X+\abs b\abs Y$.
(For random variables on a general probability space, linearity is proved in Chapter 15; the statement is the same.)
If $X\ge0$ then $\Exp[X]\ge0$, with equality if and only if $\Prob(X=0)=1$.
(Monotonicity) If $X\le Y$ then $\Exp[X]\le\Exp[Y]$.
$\abs{\Exp[X]}\le\Exp\abs X$.
$\Exp[\indic_A]=\Prob(A)$.
(Tail-sum formula) If $X$ takes values in $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$, then $\Exp[X]=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\Prob(X\ge k)$.

(i) Each term $xp(x)$ with $x\ge0$ is non-negative; the sum is $0$ only if every $x>0$ has $p(x)=0$. (ii) $Y-X\ge0$, so by (i) and linearity $\Exp[Y]-\Exp[X]\ge0$. (iii) Apply (ii) to $-\abs X\le X\le\abs X$. (iv) $\indic_A$ takes value $1$ with probability $\Prob(A)$ and $0$ otherwise.

(v) Write $X=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\indic_{\{X\ge k\}}$: for an outcome with $X=m$, the indicators for $k=1,\dots,m$ equal $1$ and the rest $0$, so the sum is $m$. Taking expectations term by term (justified because all terms are non-negative, so we may interchange the double sum $\sum_k\sum_x$) gives the formula:
\sum_{k\ge1}\Prob(X\ge k)=\sum_{k\ge1}\sum_{x\ge k}p(x)=\sum_{x\ge1}p(x)\sum_{k=1}^{x}1=\sum_xx\,p(x).
The indicator method
Linearity plus indicators gives a way to compute expectations of counts without finding their distributions.

To find $\Exp[N]$ for a count $N$: write $N=\sum_i\indic_{A_i}$ where each $A_i$ is the event that item $i$ “counts”, then $\Exp[N]=\sum_i\Prob(A_i)$. Dependence among the $A_i$ is irrelevant. This single idea solves a large fraction of expectation questions in interviews.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Fixed points of a random permutation

blocks.x: Let $N$ be the number of fixed points of a uniformly random permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (the matching problem, Example 2.8). With $A_i=\{\text{position }i\text{ is fixed}\}$, $\Prob(A_i)=(n-1)!/n!=1/n$, so $\Exp[N]=n\cdot\frac1n=1$ for every $n$. Compare with the effort needed to find the distribution of $N$; here we get the mean in one line, even though the $A_i$ are dependent.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be a uniformly random ordering of $n$ distinct numbers. Say position $k$ is a record if $x_k$ exceeds all earlier values. Let $R_k$ indicate a record at position $k$. By symmetry, the largest among the first $k$ values is equally likely to be in any of the $k$ positions, so $\Prob(R_k=1)=1/k$. Hence the expected number of records is the harmonic number

\Exp\Bigl[\sum_kR_k\Bigr]=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac1k=H_n\approx\ln n+\gamma,\qquad
\gamma\approx0.5772 .
For $n=100$ this is about $5.19$: a record-setting streak stays rare.

The mean describes the centre of a distribution. The variance measures its spread.
If $\Exp[X^2]<\infty$, the variance of $X$ is $\Var(X)=\Exp\bigl[(X-\mu)^2\bigr]$, where $\mu=\Exp[X]$. The standard deviation is $\sigma_X=\sqrt{\Var(X)}$.
(Finite second moment implies finite first moment, because $\abs x\le(1+x^2)/2$.)
$\Var(aX+b)=a^2\Var(X)$.
$\Var(X)=0$ if and only if $\Prob(X=\mu)=1$.
For any constant $c$, $\Exp[(X-c)^2]=\Var(X)+(\mu-c)^2$; hence the mean is the constant that minimises the mean squared deviation.
(i) Expand $(X-\mu)^2=X^2-2\mu X+\mu^2$ and use linearity: $\Exp[X^2]-2\mu\cdot\mu+\mu^2=\Exp[X^2]-\mu^2$. Non-negativity holds because $(X-\mu)^2\ge0$.
(ii) $aX+b$ has mean $a\mu+b$, so $(aX+b)-(a\mu+b)=a(X-\mu)$ and its square has expectation $a^2\Var(X)$.
(iii) By Proposition 4.16(i), $\Exp[(X-\mu)^2]=0$ exactly when $(X-\mu)^2=0$ almost surely.
(iv) $(X-c)^2=((X-\mu)+(\mu-c))^2=(X-\mu)^2+2(\mu-c)(X-\mu)+(\mu-c)^2$. Taking expectations, the middle term vanishes since $\Exp[X-\mu]=0$.
For $X=\indic_A$ with $p=\Prob(A)$: $X^2=X$, so $\Var(X)=p-p^2=p(1-p)$. This is maximised at $p=1/2$.

Linearity of expectation holds always, but variance is additive only when the variables are uncorrelated (in particular, when independent). We prove the exact formula in Chapter 6. Also, $\Var(-X)=\Var(X)$, not $-\Var(X)$.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: the mean need not be a value $X$ can take

blocks.x: A fair die has $\Exp[X]=3.5$, which is not a possible outcome. The mean is a long-run average, not a “typical” value. The median and mode can be more representative for skewed distributions, and for heavy-tailed variables (Example 4.12) the mean may not exist at all.
Find the PMF, mean and variance of the sum of two fair dice. (Use linearity for the mean.)
Let $X$ have CDF $F(x)=0$ for $x<1$, $F(x)=0.3$ for $1\le x<3$, $F(x)=0.7$ for $3\le x<5$, and $F(x)=1$ for $x\ge5$. Find the PMF and $\Prob(2<X\le5)$.
Prove that if $X$ takes values in $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ then $\Exp[X^2]=\sum_{k\ge1}(2k-1)\Prob(X\ge k)$.
A deck of $n$ cards numbered $1,\dots,n$ is shuffled and the cards are turned over one at a time. Find the expected number of times a card is immediately followed by a card with a larger number.
(Expected number of distinct values) Roll a fair die $n$ times. Find the expected number of faces that appear at least once. (Indicator for each face.)

(Cycle structure) In a uniformly random permutation of $n$ elements, show that the expected number of cycles is $H_n$. (Hint: build the permutation by the “fundamental bijection” or compute the expected number of cycles of length $k$.)
Show that $\Var(X)\le\Exp[(X-c)^2]$ for every constant $c$, and use this to show that if $a\le X\le b$ then $\Var(X)\le(b-a)^2/4$.
Let $X$ take values in $\{1,2,\dots\}$ with $\Prob(X=k)=\frac{6}{\pi^2k^2}$. Show that $\Exp[X]=\infty$ but $\Prob(X<\infty)=1$.
(Challenge) Prove that the indicators $R_1,\dots,R_n$ of Example 4.18 are mutually independent, and conclude that the variance of the number of records is $\sum_k\frac1k(1-\frac1k)$.
